title: Which wrapper to use, and when an adapter is not needed

questions.stem: A class holds an XmlDataSource and implements JsonDataSource, which your code already calls. Which pattern is it?

options.text: A Decorator: it holds an XmlDataSource behind JsonDataSource to add work to each call.
options.says: A decorator keeps the same interface as the object it wraps and adds behaviour; this class presents a different interface.

options.text: A Facade: it holds an XmlDataSource behind JsonDataSource to offer a simpler API.
options.says: A facade sits in front of a subsystem of many objects; this class wraps a single source and converts its interface.

options.text: An Adapter: it holds an XmlDataSource behind JsonDataSource to translate each call.
options.says: The page's XmlToJsonAdapter is its own example: it lets an existing class be used where a different interface is expected.

questions.stem: Your team owns both DataFetcher and the client code that calls it, and their methods do not match. What does the page suggest?

options.text: Since you own both sides, change the fetcher's signature to suit the clients.
options.says: The page's Q6 says an adapter is not worth its extra layer when you control both interfaces: you align them instead.

options.text: Since you own both sides, write an object adapter so that neither side changes.
options.says: The page keeps adapters for code you cannot modify, such as a third-party search engine; here both sides can be changed.

options.text: Since you own both sides, write a class adapter that inherits the fetcher's code.
options.says: A class adapter still adds the extra layer the page wants to avoid, and it ties the adapter to one class through inheritance.
